Memorandum

To:	Public Utility Commission of Texas
From:	Jeff McDonald; Michael Reinisch
Date:	August 11, 2026
Re:	IMM Commentary on Rulemaking for Transmission Cost Recovery P-58000
Introduction
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule in Project 58000 on the Commission’s proposed revisions to the way transmission costs are recovered in ERCOT. Reforming the 4 Coincident Peak (4CP) methodology may address the oldest remaining recommendation in our annual State of the Market report. We first made this recommendation in 2015, when the 4CP framework was already materially affecting wholesale market price formation and allowing certain market participants to avoid responsibility for costs they imposed.
In these comments, we discuss the interplay between transmission cost allocation and the wholesale market, describe the mechanics of the existing 4CP methodology, and distinguish the theoretical benefits attributed to coincident-peak allocation from the concrete market distortions and cost-allocation problems that have resulted from its use. We then evaluate the proposed 12CP methodology and present an alternative framework for allocating transmission costs. We conclude with several observations on specific aspects of the proposed rule.
Transmission Cost Allocation & the Wholesale Market
Transmission cost allocation intersects with wholesale market outcomes at many junctures. Real-time transmission scarcity is reflected directly in congestion pricing, which affects both load costs and generator revenues. Transmission availability and cost also influence where loads and generators choose to locate, which in turn affects resource adequacy, deliverability, and the future need for transmission expansion. In addition, when customers can reduce or avoid transmission charges through behavior in the wholesale market, that behavior affects price formation in both the energy and ancillary services markets by changing demand in intervals that may not otherwise reflect customers’ underlying willingness to consume or the system’s marginal cost of serving load.
The 4CP Method
Mechanism and Perceived Benefits
The 4CP methodology allocates transmission costs to distribution service providers (DSPs) based on each DSP’s share of total ERCOT demand during the 15-minute coincident peak intervals in June, July, August, and September. Because a DSP’s future transmission charges depend on its load during those four intervals, the methodology creates a strong incentive for load to reduce consumption during anticipated monthly peak hours, a behavior known as 4CP response. The premise underlying this structure is that system peak demand is an appropriate proxy for the transmission costs caused by load, and that reducing demand during those limited peak conditions can defer transmission capacity that would otherwise be needed primarily to serve rare system-peak events.
Drawbacks of 4CP 
Beyond the fairness concern that 4CP allows certain loads to avoid paying their share of transmission costs, a key drawback of the methodology is its effect on wholesale market price formation. In the many intervals when loads anticipate a possible coincident peak and self-curtail to reduce future transmission charges, demand is reduced for reasons unrelated to real-time energy or ancillary service prices. In earlier years, when ERCOT had fewer renewable resources and tight system conditions more often coincided with gross peak demand, this behavior was more likely to overlap with intervals in which high prices reflected actual generation scarcity. Today, as the gap between gross peak demand and net peak demand has widened, 4CP-driven load response increasingly occurs to avoid transmission charges rather than in response to wholesale prices signaling scarcity.
Testing the Assumptions
This framing produces an unresolved tension in the case for CP-based allocation. CP response is treated as beneficial because it is assumed to reduce demand during transmission scarcity and defer future transmission investment, yet the same response is also recognized as problematic when it allows certain loads to avoid paying transmission costs and distorts wholesale market price formation. The prevailing view appears to be that some CP response is good, but too much CP response is bad. Proponents of a CP methodology therefore assume that the transmission-planning benefits of CP response outweigh the fairness concerns and wholesale market impacts associated with that behavior. That assumption is central to the proposed 12CP framework discussed below, but the perceived benefit that is foundational to the CP methodology has never been substantiated.
The Commission Staff report filed in Project 58484 provides the analytical foundation for the proposed rule and continues to rely on that same premise. The report treats peak demand as the primary driver of transmission investment, but it does not test whether reductions during CP intervals actually defer or avoid transmission projects, nor does it provide empirical support for that conclusion. If system peak demand were a reliable indicator of transmission scarcity, that scarcity should be observable systematically in real-time congestion pricing. As we have explained in prior filings on this issue, the correlation between peak demand and congestion pricing is weak, which suggests that CP intervals are at best an incomplete proxy for the transmission constraints that drive actual system costs. Before preserving and expanding an incentive that affects behavior in the energy and ancillary services markets, the Commission should require evidence that CP-driven demand reductions actually reduce long-term transmission costs.
Actual Drivers of Transmission Costs
Transmission costs are driven by more than coincident peak demand. The principal drivers are the obligation to serve new or reserved load, demand under planning-relevant peak or stressed conditions, reliability upgrades needed to address thermal, voltage, stability, and contingency issues, and the location of generation and load across the grid. The Commission Staff report recognizes many of these factors, including large-load growth, winter peaks, shoulder-season maintenance constraints, local generation imbalances, and ERCOT-identified reliability projects. Those factors may overlap with system peak demand, but they are not equivalent to it. A CP methodology therefore risks treating a convenient billing proxy as though it were a demonstrated measure of transmission cost causation. 
A comprehensive cost-causation methodology would need to account for each of these drivers, which would necessarily be more complex than a CP-based allocator. But if the Commission adopts a methodology that materially influences behavior in the wholesale market, the methodology should be supported by evidence that the induced behavior actually reduces transmission costs. A methodology that encourages market participants to chase transmission-charge avoidance based on perceived system benefits does not necessarily improve cost causation. It may simply replace one imperfect allocation method with another, while continuing to distort wholesale market outcomes.
Comments on the Proposed Rule: 12CP and Beyond
The proposed rule would make several significant changes to transmission cost allocation, including replacing 4CP with 12CP, expanding the measurement interval from 15 minutes to 30 minutes, eliminating interconnection allowances by requiring direct interconnection costs to be recovered through a load’s contribution in aid of construction (CIAC), and introducing a minimum billing demand that would hold large loads accountable for contracted peak demand when that value exceeds the customer’s 12CP or NCP demand. We generally support the use of a minimum billing demand and the recovery of more direct interconnection costs through CIAC, as discussed later in this document. Our principal concern is with the proposed 12CP design, which remains grounded in a coincident-peak framework that does not adequately reflect the drivers of transmission cost causation.
Flaws with 12CP 
The 12CP methodology was proposed in the Commission Staff report filed in Project No. 58484. In that report, Staff analyzed a relatively narrow set of coincident-peak alternatives, principally ranging from 5CP to 12CP, with supplemental consideration of 52CP and 365CP methodologies. Staff rejected the broader 52CP and 365CP approaches largely because they would dilute, and potentially eliminate, the incentive for CP-based demand response. But the value of preserving that incentive is assumed rather than demonstrated. The report does not test whether CP-driven load reductions actually defer or avoid transmission investment, identify transmission projects that were avoided because of CP response, or otherwise support the assumed transmission-cost benefit with empirical data or other evidence. 
Any CP will Preserve the Avoidance Incentive
The proposed 12CP methodology may make it somewhat more difficult for loads to reduce their transmission-cost allocation, but it does not eliminate the incentive to do so. The commercial value of accurately forecasting CP intervals will remain substantial, and the existing industry that supports CP prediction and avoidance has every reason to adapt its tools, models, and customer strategies to a 12CP framework. Expanding the methodology from four intervals to twelve would therefore increase the number of periods in which loads attempt to reduce consumption for the purpose of avoiding transmission charges, because the financial incentive to do so would remain highly profitable. This would also expand the wholesale market impacts of CP response by creating more intervals in which load reductions are driven by transmission-cost avoidance rather than by energy or ancillary service prices.
Minimum Billing Demand
Under the proposed rule, a new large load customer would be billed based on the greater of its contracted peak demand, its highest NCP demand, or its 12CP demand. That obligation would begin when service becomes available, regardless of whether the customer has energized or is fully using the available capacity and would continue for 20 years. In practical terms, the minimum billing demand delays a new large load customer’s ability to avoid transmission charges through 12CP response during that 20-year period.
That approach is directionally appropriate, but incomplete. It reduces the incentive for new large loads to overstate capacity needs and then avoid charges through CP response, but it does not eliminate the underlying flaw in the 12CP methodology. It largely postpones the opportunity for new large loads to game the allocation method, and it does nothing to address existing loads that can continue to reduce their transmission-cost responsibility through CP avoidance.
We nevertheless support the use of a minimum billing demand because it better aligns cost responsibility with the capacity a customer requests and the transmission investment needed to serve that request. It also gives large loads an incentive to right-size their interconnection requests, which should improve load forecasting and reduce the risk of stranded or underutilized transmission investment. In the next section, we propose an alternative framework that incorporates minimum billing demand while more directly addressing the deficiencies of CP-based allocation.
Contribution in Aid of Construction
We generally support the beneficiary-pays principle reflected in the proposed CIAC provisions. Assigning direct interconnection costs to the large load customer that causes those costs is more consistent with cost causation and reduces the risk of socializing customer-specific costs through TCOS, which in turn lessens the resulting distortions to wholesale market price formation. We do not take a position here on the specific costs that should be included in CIAC, but it would be useful to understand the approximate extent to which this policy is expected to reduce the TCOS recovered through the final allocation methodology.
IMM Proposal for Transmission Cost Allocation
Allocate Transmission Costs According to Load-Ratio Share
The alternative we propose is to replace coincident-peak allocation with a load-ratio share methodology. Rather than assigning transmission costs based on consumption during a limited set of forecastable intervals, load-ratio share would allocate those costs based on each load’s share of total system demand over a broader period. This simple change would fully address the concerns raised in our State of the Market reports over the past decade by removing the incentive to alter wholesale market behavior solely to avoid transmission charges. The framework could also incorporate a minimum billing demand and would eliminate the avoidance opportunity for existing and new loads of any size, rather than addressing only new large loads.
Minimum Billing Demand
We support incorporating a minimum billing demand into a load-ratio share framework because it would assign greater cost responsibility to large loads whose capacity requests are expected to drive substantial transmission investment, while preserving their incentive to right-size those requests. For each large load, the framework could calculate minimum energy consumption by applying its contracted capacity to an agreed load profile and measuring the resulting MWh over the allocation period. The customer’s transmission allocation would then be based on the greater of this minimum consumption or its actual consumption.
Congestion Impact
Eliminating the CP-avoidance incentive would allow demand during peak periods to reflect actual consumption decisions rather than artificial efforts to reduce future transmission charges. Because congestion pricing has some correlation with peak demand, this could result in higher congestion prices during certain peak intervals that would otherwise be affected by CP response. Those higher prices would not reflect a flaw in the methodology. They would restore a market signal that is currently being suppressed. More accurate congestion prices would better inform generation and energy storage developers where new resources can provide the greatest value by relieving transmission constraints.
Comments Specific to Commission Questions
Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different noncoincident (NCP) demands?
If the Commission continues with a CP-based allocation approach, we take no strong position on whether minimum billing demand values should vary based on a large load customer’s contracted peak demand or NCP demand. We note, however, that demand magnitude alone does not determine the operational burden a large load places on the transmission system. Rapid changes in demand over short periods may create more significant operational challenges, including the need for additional voltage support and other facilities necessary to reliably interconnect and serve the load. Any differentiation among large load customers should therefore consider ramping characteristics and resulting system costs, rather than relying solely on demand magnitude.
Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
 fixed for 20 years as proposed; 
reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or 
extended to a longer time period? 
We take no strong position on the appropriate duration or phase-down of the minimum billing demand. We support the requirement because it incentivizes large loads to right-size their capacity requests. That incentive would be preserved under either a fixed 20-year obligation phased reduction over the same period. However, under a phased reduction over 20 years, the cost avoidance incentive would be gradually reinstated. For that reason, we do not advocate for a phased reduction. We defer to other stakeholders on whether extending the obligation beyond 20 years is necessary.
Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large load minimum billing demand: 
reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is some percentage of the customer' s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in phases over the years, and how? 
be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load customer' s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous year and the large load customer's 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases over the years, and how? 
We take no strong position on whether the minimum billing demand should be ratcheted, weighted, or reduced over time, provided the selected approach preserves a meaningful incentive for large load customers to right-size their capacity requests.
Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and cryptocurrency mining facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large computational loads. 
We recognize concerns regarding the uncertainty associated with large computational loads, including the risk that their interconnection costs may be shifted to other customers and that they may not remain on the system long enough to contribute fully to the recovery of the costs they cause. We are skeptical, however, that separate rate treatment based solely on the nature or purpose of the load would effectively address those concerns. If separate treatment is warranted, distinctions based on measurable operational characteristics or performance, such as rapid ramping behavior or failures to ride through voltage disturbances may be more appropriate. We take no position on whether the Commission should adopt separate rate treatment or on the specific form that treatment should take.
Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load? 
We take no position on the specific facilities or cost categories that should be included within the definition of transmission interconnection costs. We generally support applying cost-causation principles so that costs attributable to serving particular loads are assigned to those loads rather than broadly socialized through TCOS. Any allocation of batch-study project costs should reasonably reflect the extent to which the affected loads caused or benefited from the project.
If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and transmission planning studies? 
Our understanding is that ERCOT’s open-access transmission framework does not provide for the formal reservation of transmission capacity by a particular load. To the extent transmission capacity is nevertheless planned and made available for a large load that falls behind its energization schedule, ERCOT’s resource adequacy reports and assessments could present a range of outcomes rather than a single forecast. That range could include one scenario reflecting the customer’s full contracted peak demand and another reflecting updated energization schedules and the observed ramp-up of interconnected loads. ERCOT used a similar scenario-based approach in the updates provided during the Batch Zero process.
Executive Summary – Potomac Economics – Independent Market Monitor
Since the 2015 State of the Market report, we have recommended replacing the 4CP methodology because it distorts wholesale market price formation and allows responsive loads to avoid transmission costs that are then shifted to other customers. The proposed 12CP methodology would not resolve these concerns. 
Avoiding transmission cost allocation is overwhelmingly profitable, and the industry supporting this behavior will continue to thrive as total transmission cost of service multiplies in the coming years. Moving from 4CP to 12CP would preserve this powerful avoidance incentive while expanding the number of periods affected by CP-driven curtailment. Instead, the incentive should be eliminated entirely, particularly because the asserted benefit that CP response defers or avoids transmission investment has never been substantiated.
Beyond the significant adverse incentives created by CP-based allocation, coincident peak demand is also a poor proxy for cost causation. As we have demonstrated in prior filings, system peak demand is only weakly correlated with real-time congestion prices and therefore does not reliably indicate transmission scarcity. Transmission investment is instead driven by a more complex set of factors, including the obligation to serve new or reserved load, demand under planning-relevant peak or stressed conditions, reliability upgrades needed to address thermal, voltage, stability, and contingency issues, and the location of generation and load across the grid. Attempting to capture each of these factors through an increasingly complex allocation methodology would likely create new behavioral incentives and further distort wholesale market outcomes.
To that end, we recommend that the Commission:
Replace coincident-peak allocation with a load-ratio share methodology. Transmission costs should be allocated based on load ratio share rather than consumption during a limited set of forecastable intervals.
Incorporate minimum billing demand into the load-ratio share framework. A large load’s allocation could be based on the greater of its actual consumption or minimum MWh derived from its contracted capacity and an agreed load profile. This would preserve the incentive to right-size capacity requests while avoiding CP-driven market distortions.
Allow congestion prices to provide accurate market signals. Eliminating artificial CP response may increase congestion prices in some peak intervals, but those prices would reveal constraints that are currently suppressed and would better signal where generation and energy storage can relieve congestion.

   4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an

We recognize concerns regarding the uncertainty associated with large computational loads,
including the risk that their interconnection costs may be shifted to other customers and that they
may not remain on the system long enough to contribute fully to the recovery ofthe costs they
cause. We are skeptical, however, that separate rate treatment based solely on the nature or
purpose of the load would effectively address those concerns. If separate treatment is warranted,
distinctions based on measurable operational characteristics or performance, such as rapid
ramping behavior or failures to ride through voltage disturbances may be more appropriate. We
take no position on whether the Commission should adopt separate rate treatment or on the
specific form that treatment should take.

G.    Executive Summary - Potomac Economics - Independent Market Monitor
Since the 2015 State ofthe Market report, we have recommended replacing the 4CP
methodology because it distorts wholesale market price formation and allows responsive loads to
avoid transmission costs that are then shifted to other customers. The proposed 12CP
methodology would not resolve these concerns.
Avoiding transmission cost allocation is overwhelmingly profitable, and the industry supporting
this behavior will continue to thrive as total transmission cost of service multiplies in the coming
years. Moving from 4CP to 12CP would preserve this powerful avoidance incentive while
expanding the number of periods affected by CP-driven curtailment. Instead, the incentive
should be eliminated entirely, particularly because the asserted benefit that CP response defers or
avoids transmission investment has never been substantiated.
Beyond the significant adverse incentives created by CP-based allocation, coincident peak
demand is also a poor proxy for cost causation. As we have demonstrated in prior filings, system
peak demand is only weakly correlated with real-time congestion prices and therefore does not
reliably indicate transmission scarcity. Transmission investment is instead driven by a more
complex set of factors, including the obligation to serve new or reserved load, demand under
planning-relevant peak or stressed conditions, reliability upgrades needed to address thermal,
voltage, stability, and contingency issues, and the location of generation and load across the grid.
Attempting to capture each of these factors through an increasingly complex allocation
methodology would likely create new behavioral incentives and further distort wholesale market
outcomes.
To that end, we recommend that the Commission:
•    Replace coincident-peak allocation with a load-ratio share methodology. Transmission
     costs should be allocated based on load ratio share rather than consumption during a limited
     set of forecastable intervals.
•    Incorporate minimum billing demand into the load-ratio share framework. A large
     load' s allocation could be based on the greater of its actual consumption or minimum MWh
     derived from its contracted capacity and an agreed load profile. This would preserve the
     incentive to right-size capacity requests while avoiding CP-driven market distortions.
•    Allow congestion prices to provide accurate market signals. Eliminating artificial CP
     response may increase congestion prices in some peak intervals, but those prices would
     reveal constraints that are currently suppressed and would better signal where generation and
     energy storage can relieve congestion.
